full_judgment:
175. In the case of Fazal Dad vs Crown reported in 1955 PLD (FC) 152 = 7 DLR (FC) 176, it has been observed that the evidence of an accomplice has to be considered as a whole, and though the Court starts with the initial presumption against his trustworthiness, it may accept his testimony if it is corroborated in material particulars. It has been further observed in that case that the Rule that insists on corroboration of the approver's evidence does not require that corroboration must be on all the particulars of the story, nor that there must be corroboration on that part of the story of the accomplice in which he has implicated himself and if the independent evidence produced in corroboration tends to show that the persons named by him were parties to the commission of the offence charged, the Court is entitled to accept his evidence even though there be no corroboration against the accomplice himself. 

 176. In the case of Abdul Qadir vs State reported in 8 DLR (SC) 165, it has been observed that the real danger in acting upon the uncorroborated evidence of an accomplice is the possibility that in the desire to screen his real partner in the crime, he may substitute for him a completely innocent man who may not know at all why he has been so substituted, and it is for this reason that the Court has never convicted a person simply on the ground that he is unable to explain why the accomplice has implicated him. 

 186. The PW 2 Md Abul Hossain appears to be a naturai and competent witness. At the relevant time, he was very much present at the scene of occurrence. If we juxtapose and consider the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination of the PW 2 Md Abul Hossain together, the lone eye-witness to the occurrence, we find that he has dourly stood his ground. The substantive part touching upon the factum of the occurrence-its manner, method and sequence-has not been shaken, deviated from or rendered doubtful in his cross-examination. It is an indubitable fact that the accused Tonmoy and Bhulu were not known to him at any point of time before the occurrence. So we do not find any earthly reason as to why he will falsely implicate the accused Tonmoy and Bhulu in the case. Reading the evidence of the PW 2 Abul Hossain as a whole, we do not come across any blemish or marks of false- hood therein. This being the situation, we are inclined to accept the evidence of the PW 2 Md Abul Hossain as true. The evidence of the approver Md Alam (PW 3) so far it relates to the mode of commission of the offence following a pre-concerted plan and the subsequent apprehension of the accused Tonmoy near the MacDonald Chinese Restaurant has been corroborated by the PW 2 Md Abul Hossain. 

 205. In support of the contention of Mr Shakawat Hossain Bahar that the accused Md Alam was not legally tendered pardon by the Court of Sessions and, as such, he cannot be examined as a witness and his evidence as an approver is wholly inadmissible in evidence, he has referred to the decision in the case of Abdur Rashid vs State reported in 22 DLR 109. But Mrs Fazilatunnessa contends that the accused Md Alam was legally pardoned and discharged and, as such, the question of inadmissibility of his evidence as an approver does not arise at all. 

 Before a Court acts upon a confessional statement, it has to affirmatively satisfy that the statement is voluntary and true. In this regard, the judicial authorities always insist on the meticulous observance of all necessary formalities and precautions provided in section 164(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure with minute particularity so as to ensure that the confession is absolutely free from the slightest tinge or taint of extraneous influence. 'It is a settled principle of law' as pointed out by a Division Bench of this Court in the case of Zaheda Bewa vs State reported in 1985 BLD 9 = 37 DLR 66 'that the requirement of adherence to the provisions of section 164(3), CrPC is not a mere matter of form, but of substance. Section 164(3) is a mandatory provision of law as has been settled by the Privy Council in the case of Nazir Ahmed vs King Emperor, AIR 1936 PC 253. Before recording a confession, a Magistrate is bound to make a real and substantial enquiry as to the voluntariness of the confession. In so doing, he must put question to the accused with a view to finding out the real object of the confession, whether it is made out of repentance or for any other such good reason or whether it is the result of torture or torturing by somebody or whether it has been caused by any inducement, threat or promise. The questions put by the Magistrate and the answers given by the accused furnish sufficient data for coming to the conclusion whether the statement was voluntary or not." 

 210. Be that as it may, Mrs Fazilatunnessa has adverted to the decision in the case of Ratan Kha @ Rattan vs State reported in 40 DLR 186 in support of her contention that any irregularity in recording the confession is curable by section 533 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 211. In the case of Nurul Haque vs Slate reported in 20 DLR 780, it has been observed: 

 As the provision of section 164(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is mandatory, any violation thereof is an illegality and not a mere irregularity. It may be pointed out that the decision reported in 40 DLR 186 referred to by Mrs Fazilatunnessa relates to an irregularity in respect of granting of time for reflection to an accused before recording his confession. However, in the present case before us, as the mandatory provision of section 164(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure was contravened by the learned Magistrate (PW 8) in recording the confessional statement of the accused Tonmoy, this contravention is definitely an illegality not curable by section 533 of the said Code. As such, the above contention of Mrs Fazilatunnessa stands discarded. 

 217. However the instant Death Reference has been pending before the High Court since 2001. By the way, the decision in the case of Abul Khair vs State reported in 44 DLR (AD) 225 may be called in aid. In that decision, it has been held in paragraph 17: 

 243. However Mr Md Amir-ul-Islam has drawn our attention to paragraph 17 in the decision in the case of Ali Akbar vs State reported in 51 DLR 268 which is as follows : 

 "17. It is now well settled by the decisions of the Federal Court and the Supreme Court of Pakistan as well as the decisions of the Appellate Division of our Supreme Court as noticed and referred to in the case of Abdul Aziz vs Sekander Ali reported in 50 DLR 111, to which one of us was a party, that merely because the Court deciding a revision against acquittal of the accused may arrive at a different conclusion on consideration of the evidence on record would not be justified in reversing the decision of the trial Court unless it is possible to demonstrate with certainty that none of the grounds upon which the trial Court acquitted the accused is at all supportable, the same being manifestly wrong or perverse." 

 244. Mr Md Amir-ul-Islam next refers to paragraph 17 in the decision in the case of Abdul Hamid Mollah vs AU Mollah reported in 44 DLR (AD) 223 which runs as under: 

 "17. However, we are deciding this case on the settled principle that unless it is possible to demonstrate with certainty that none of the grounds upon which the learned Judges have purported to acquit is at all supportable, this Court will be reluctant to interfere, even though upon the evidence on the record and the facts and circumstances of the case, this Court might well have come to a different conclusion if it was trying the case. This principle has been referred to by Hamoodur Rahman J in the case of Siraj Din vs Kala 16 DLR (SC) 94."
